question: How do you set SDR quotas that are actually attainable in 2027?
body:
## Direct Answer Attainable SDR quotas in 2027 are built bottom-up from capacity math, not top-down from a revenue gap: start with the meetings a fully-ramped rep can realistically book given your funnel conversion rates, then discount for ramp, tenure mix, seasonality, and territory quality. A healthy target is one where roughly 60–70% of your ramped reps clear quota in a normal quarter — high enough to stretch, low enough that the plan stays believable and reps don't churn. Most SDR quotas are unattainable because they are set backwards. Leadership picks a pipeline number the business needs, divides it by headcount, and calls the result a quota — with no reference to how many dials, emails, and conversations it would actually take to get there, or whether the reps have the ramp, data, and inbound support to hit it. In 2027, with AI-assisted prospecting compressing some activity while buyer saturation makes cold outreach harder, the only defensible way to set a number is to model it from the bottom up and pressure-test it against your own historical conversion data. This essay walks through the capacity model, the attainment-distribution target, the ramp and seasonality adjustments, and the governance cadence that keeps the number honest quarter over quarter. ## What does "attainable" actually mean for an SDR quota? Attainable does not mean easy, and it does not mean everyone hits it. A quota that 100% of reps clear is a quota set too low — you're leaving pipeline and motivation on the table, and your top performers have no reason to push. A quota that only 20% of reps clear is not a stretch goal; it's a resignation letter you're handing your team on a delay. The industry-recognized healthy band is roughly **60–70% of fully-ramped reps attaining quota in a typical period**, with a meaningful spread above and below that midpoint. That distribution tells you the number is calibrated to real capacity with genuine headroom for excellence. The second dimension of attainability is *controllability*. SDRs should be measured on the things they can actually influence — meetings booked, qualified opportunities created, sequences completed — not on downstream outcomes like closed-won revenue that depend on AE skill, pricing, and deal cycles they don't touch. When you quota an SDR on closed revenue, you've made their income a function of another person's job. That's the fastest route to disengagement and gaming. Attainable quotas are set on the metric closest to the SDR's daily work while still being a leading indicator of revenue: typically **qualified meetings held** or **accepted opportunities**, not raw meetings booked (which invites no-show inflation) and not closed deals (which they don't control). For a deeper treatment of which stage to anchor on, see the funnel-metric breakdown at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sdr-funnel-metrics. ## How do you build the quota from the bottom up? Bottom-up capacity modeling is the core of an attainable quota. Instead of starting from the revenue target, you start from the rep and work forward through your own conversion rates. The logic is a chain: available selling hours → activities per hour → conversations per activity → meetings per conversation → qualified opportunities per meeting. Each link is a rate you pull from your CRM history, not a number you wish for. Here is the flow of the capacity model, from a rep's working capacity down to the quota-bearing outcome: ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Selling days per quarter
minus PTO, training, holidays] --> B[Daily activity capacity
dials + emails + social touches] B --> C[Connect / reply rate
from CRM history] C --> D[Conversations held] D --> E[Meeting booking rate] E --> F[Meetings booked] F --> G[Show + qualification rate] G --> H[Qualified opportunities
= the quota metric] H --> I{60-70% of ramped reps
clear this number?} I -->|No, too high| J[Lower target or
fix a funnel constraint] I -->|No, too low| K[Raise target,
capture upside] I -->|Yes| L[Set as quota] ``` Work a concrete example. Suppose your CRM shows a fully-ramped SDR realistically sustains a certain daily activity volume, that a known percentage of those touches turn into live conversations, and that a known share of conversations convert to a booked meeting. Multiply the chain across the ~55–60 true selling days in a quarter (after you subtract PTO, holidays, all-hands, and training), and you arrive at a *modeled* meeting number. Apply your historical show-and-qualify rate, and you get modeled qualified opportunities. **That modeled output — not a revenue-gap division — is your starting quota.** The revenue target then becomes a *check*: if the bottom-up capacity across the whole team can't produce the pipeline the business needs, the answer is to hire, raise conversion, or improve data — not to inflate the per-rep number until the spreadsheet balances. A quota that only reconciles the revenue gap on paper is a quota that will miss in reality. The discipline here is using *your* rates, not benchmark averages. Published benchmarks from sources like The Bridge Group's SDR reports are useful sanity checks and directional guides, but your connect rates depend on your ICP, your data quality, your dialer, and your brand recognition. A well-known brand in a warm category converts cold outreach at multiples of an unknown startup in a saturated one. Borrowing someone else's conversion rate is how you manufacture an unattainable number that looked perfectly reasonable in the model. ## How do ramp, tenure, and seasonality change the number? A quota that ignores ramp is a quota that punishes every new hire and every manager who's growing a team. New SDRs are not productive on day one; they climb a ramp curve as they learn the product, the ICP, the objections, and the tools. The standard practice is **prorated or stepped quotas during the ramp period** — commonly a 3-to-4-month glide for SDRs — where the target scales up month over month until it reaches the full-tenure number. Charging a month-two rep the full quota guarantees a miss, distorts your attainment distribution, and burns comp on a target no reasonable person expected them to hit. The tenure mix of your team then rolls up into the plan. If half your team ramped this quarter, the *team* pipeline target has to reflect that reality — you cannot model the team as if every seat is a fully-ramped veteran. Seasonality compounds this: December and late summer are structurally slower for outbound in most B2B markets because buyers are out of office and budgets are in flux, while the back half of Q1 and Q3 tend to run hot. Attainable quarterly quotas are **seasonally weighted**, not the annual number divided by four. Flat-lining the quarters means you set an impossible bar in the slow quarter and an under-ambitious one in the peak. Here's how the raw capacity number gets adjusted into a per-rep, per-quarter quota: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Base capacity quota
from bottom-up model] --> B[Ramp multiplier
0.25 -> 0.5 -> 0.75 -> 1.0
by tenure month] A --> C[Seasonality index
slow quarter < 1.0
peak quarter > 1.0] A --> D[Territory quality factor
enterprise vs SMB,
data density, inbound share] B --> E[Adjusted per-rep quota] C --> E D --> E E --> F[Roll up to team target] F --> G[Reconcile vs pipeline need] ``` Territory quality is the adjustment teams most often skip and most often regret. Two reps with identical skill will post wildly different numbers if one works a dense, high-intent, inbound-fed territory and the other works cold accounts in a thin data region. **Equal quotas across unequal territories is inequity dressed up as fairness.** Attainable quota design either balances territories before assigning equal numbers, or assigns differentiated numbers that reflect the real opportunity in each patch. For the mechanics of scoring and balancing territories, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/territory-design-revops. ## What's different about setting SDR quotas in 2027? Two structural forces reshape SDR quota-setting for 2027, and they pull in opposite directions. First, **AI-assisted prospecting has compressed the activity side of the funnel.** Research, list-building, first-draft personalization, and sequence management that used to eat hours of an SDR's day are increasingly automated. In principle this raises capacity — a rep can run more targeted plays in the same hours. But that only translates to quota if the *conversion* side holds up, and here the second force cuts the other way. Second, **buyer saturation and inbox fatigue have depressed cold-outreach response rates** across most B2B categories. When every competitor is sending AI-personalized sequences at scale, the marginal cold email converts worse than it did three years ago, and email deliverability regimes have tightened in response to volume. The net effect is that raw activity volume is a weaker predictor of pipeline than it used to be, and quality-of-targeting matters more. Practically, this means 2027 quotas should lean harder on **qualified-opportunity outcomes and account-based signals** than on activity counts, and the capacity model's conversion rates must be pulled from *recent* data — a connect rate from 2024 will over-promise today. Teams that kept quotas flat while conversion quietly eroded are the ones now staring at 30% attainment and blaming the reps. The other 2027 shift is the blurring of the SDR role itself. Where AI handles more of the top-of-funnel mechanics, the human SDR's differentiated value moves toward live conversation, complex qualification, and multi-threading — work that is lower-volume and higher-value per unit. Quota design should follow the role: if you're asking SDRs to do fewer, deeper touches on higher-fit accounts, quota them on the quality outcome (qualified opps, multi-threaded accounts) and resist the temptation to also hold them to a legacy activity floor that assumes the old high-volume motion. Holding both at once is how you get reps gaming activity metrics to survive while the pipeline number they actually own goes unmet. The connective tissue between activity design and outcome quotas is covered at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sdr-comp-plan-design. ## How do you keep the quota honest over time? A quota is not a document you set in January and revisit in December. It's a hypothesis about capacity that you test every quarter against what actually happened. The governance cadence that keeps quotas attainable is a **quarterly recalibration** anchored on the attainment distribution: pull the percentage of ramped reps who cleared quota, and read it as a signal. Consistently above ~75% attainment means the number is too soft — you're under-driving pipeline and probably overpaying against plan. Consistently below ~50% means the number is too hard, and you should expect churn and disengagement to follow if you don't act. The critical discipline is diagnosing *why* before you move the number. Low attainment can mean the quota is too high, but it can equally mean a funnel constraint the reps don't own: bad data, a broken inbound handoff, an AE team that isn't taking the meetings, a product-market shift that killed a key segment. **Moving the quota to fix a funnel problem just relocates the failure** — the pipeline still doesn't materialize, and now your best reps are demoralized *and* leaving. Attainable quota governance separates "the target is wrong" from "the machine feeding the target is broken," and fixes the actual cause. When you do change a quota, communicate the model behind it: reps accept a number they can see was built from real math far more readily than one that appears to have descended from a spreadsheet in finance. Finally, tie the quota to the comp plan's mechanics so attainability and pay stay coherent. If 65% of reps hit quota, your accelerators, thresholds, and pipeline-per-dollar economics should all be modeled against *that* distribution, not against an aspirational 90%. A quota and a comp plan that were designed in separate rooms will contradict each other the first quarter reality intrudes. ## Related questions ### What percentage of SDRs should hit quota? Roughly 60–70% of fully-ramped SDRs clearing quota in a normal period signals a well-calibrated target — high enough to stretch top performers, low enough to stay believable and retain the middle of the team. ### Should SDR quotas be based on meetings or revenue? Anchor on the outcome closest to the SDR's control that still leads revenue — usually qualified meetings held or accepted opportunities. Quotaing SDRs on closed revenue ties their pay to the AE's job and invites disengagement. ### How long should an SDR ramp period be? Most teams use a 3-to-4-month ramp with stepped, prorated quotas that scale up monthly to the full number. Charging full quota before ramp completes guarantees misses and distorts your attainment data. ### How often should you adjust SDR quotas? Recalibrate quarterly against the actual attainment distribution, but diagnose the cause before moving the number — low attainment often reflects a funnel constraint (data, handoff, AE capacity) the reps don't control, not a quota that's too high. ### How has AI changed SDR quota-setting? AI has raised activity capacity by automating research and personalization, while buyer saturation has lowered cold-outreach conversion. The net effect pushes 2027 quotas toward quality outcomes and away from raw activity volume, using recent conversion data. ## FAQ **What is a bottom-up SDR quota model?** It's a quota built by chaining your own historical conversion rates — selling days, daily activities, connect rate, meeting-booking rate, show-and-qualify rate — to arrive at a modeled outcome number. The revenue target then becomes a check on that capacity, not the source of the quota. It's the opposite of dividing a revenue gap by headcount. **Why do most SDR quotas fail to be attainable?** Because they're set top-down: leadership picks a pipeline number the business needs and divides by heads, with no reference to how many activities it takes to produce that pipeline or whether ramp, data, and territory quality support it. The number reconciles the spreadsheet but not reality. **Should new SDRs get the same quota as tenured reps?** No. Use stepped, prorated ramp quotas that scale month over month across a 3-to-4-month glide until reaching the full-tenure number. Full quota during ramp guarantees misses and skews your attainment distribution, making the whole plan look broken when it's just mis-timed. **How do you account for seasonality in SDR quotas?** Weight the quarters instead of dividing the annual number by four. Slow quarters (often December and late summer) get an index below 1.0; peak quarters get an index above 1.0. Flat quarterly targets set an impossible bar in the slow season and an under-ambitious one in the peak. **What attainment rate means a quota is too high?** If fewer than roughly half your ramped reps clear quota over consecutive periods, the number is likely too high — expect churn and disengagement to follow. But diagnose first: low attainment can also mean a broken funnel (bad data, failed inbound handoff, AEs not taking meetings) that moving the quota won't fix. **Should SDRs be measured on activities or outcomes in 2027?** Lean toward outcomes — qualified opportunities and account signals — because AI has weakened the link between raw activity volume and pipeline while buyer saturation has cut cold-response rates. Activity floors still have coaching value for new reps, but don't stack a legacy activity quota on top of an outcome quota; that just drives gaming. **How do territory differences affect quota fairness?** Two equally skilled reps post very different numbers if one works dense, high-intent, inbound-fed accounts and the other works thin cold territory. Either balance territories before assigning equal quotas or assign differentiated numbers that reflect real opportunity. Equal quotas across unequal patches is inequity disguised as fairness. **Can you use industry benchmarks to set SDR quotas?** Use them as directional sanity checks, not as inputs. Your connect and conversion rates depend on your ICP, data quality, dialer, and brand recognition, and can differ from published averages by multiples. Borrowing another company's conversion rate is a common way to build an unattainable quota that looked reasonable in the model. ## Sources - [The Bridge Group — SDR Metrics & Compensation Research](https://bridgegroupinc.com/) - [Gartner for Sales — Sales Performance and Quota Research](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales) - [Salesforce — State of Sales Report](https://www.salesforce.com/resources/research-reports/state-of-sales/) - [HubSpot Sales Blog — Quota and SDR Benchmarks](https://blog.hubspot.com/sales) - [Pavilion — Revenue Leadership Community and Benchmarks](https://www.joinpavilion.com/) - [Salesloft — Sales Engagement and SDR Productivity Research](https://salesloft.com/resources/) - [RevOps Co-op — Revenue Operations Community Resources](https://www.revopscoop.com/) - [Harvard Business Review — Sales Quota and Motivation Research](https://hbr.org/topic/sales) ## Related on PULSE - [SDR funnel metrics: which stage to quota on](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sdr-funnel-metrics) - [Territory design and balancing for RevOps](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/territory-design-revops) - [SDR comp plan design and accelerators](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sdr-comp-plan-design) - [Capacity modeling for revenue planning](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/capacity-planning-revops) - [Quota attainment distribution and plan health](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/quota-attainment-benchmarks)
